{{Short description|American physicist}}
'''Steven Michael Errede''' (born December 24, 1952) is an American experimental physicist, known for his leadership in the collaboration that experimentally confirmed the existence of the [[top quark]].<ref name=bio>{{cite web|title=Steven Michael Errede, High Energy Physics|website=University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign|url=https://physics.illinois.edu/people/directory/profile/serrede}}</ref>

==Biography==
Errede received in 1976 his B.S. from the [[University of Minnesota]].<ref name=inspirehep>{{cite web|title=Michael Steven Errede|website=inspirehep.net|url=https://inspirehep.net/authors/1010618}}</ref> For some time he worked at the University of Minnesota's Space Science Center on electronic payloads for sounding rockets used in studying the composition and magnetic field of Earth's upper atmosphere.<ref name=bio/> In 1976 he became a graduate student in physics at [[Ohio State University]], where he graduated with a Ph.D. in 1981.<ref name=inspirehep/> From 1981 to 1984 he was a postdoc at the [[University of Michigan]], where he worked on the [[Irvine-Michigan-Brookhaven (detector)|IMB Proton Decay Experiment]]. At the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]] (UIUC), he was from 1984 to 1989 an assistant professor and from 1989 to 1992 an associate professor and is since 1992 a full professor.<ref name=bio/>

Errede and his team worked on the [[ATLAS experiment]] at [[CERN]]'s [[Large Hadron Collider]] in Geneva, Switzerland. His research team built a major portion of the ATLAS experiment's Scintillating Tile Hadronic Calorimeter, used in the 2012 discovery of the [[Higgs boson]].<ref name=bio/>

In 1985 he was awarded a [[Sloan Research Fellowship]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/03/10/nyregion/90-scientists-and-economists-win-sloan-research-awards.html|title=90 Scientists and Economists Win Sloan Research Awards|date=March 10, 1985|newspaper=The New York Times|page=45B, Section 1}}</ref> In 1995 he was elected a fellow of the APS in recognition of his "contributions to the understanding of the nature of the weak gauge bosons."<ref>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1995&unit_id=&institution=University+of+Illinois}} (search on year=1995 and institution=University of Illinois)</ref>

In 2013 he won the UIUC's [[Arnold Nordsieck|Nordsieck]] Award for excellence in teaching physics. Errede developed laboratory equipment used in his teaching of undergraduate courses on acoustical physics and physics of musical instruments.<ref>{{cite web|title=Errede to receive Nordsieck Award at today's colloquium|date=May 1, 2013|website=University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Physics News|url=https://physics.illinois.edu/news/34405}}</ref><ref name=bio/>

His wife is Deborah M. Errede, who has a Ph.D. in physics from the University of Michigan.<ref>{{cite web|title=Dr Deborah M. Errede, Department of Physics at Urbana-Champaign|website=AZoQuantum|url=https://www.azoquantum.com/experts.aspx?iExpertID=371}}</ref> His father, Louis A. Errede (1923–2017), had a PhD in [[organic chemistry]] from the University of Michigan and worked for [[3M|3M Company]].<ref>{{cite book|title=The Michigan Alumnus|date=March 1963|volume=LXIX|issue=6|page=201|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lvLhAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA201}}</ref> Steven and Deborah Errede have worked together for many years and have a daughter Rachel.<ref>{{cite news|title=Louis Anthony Errede 1923–2017|newspaper=Pioneer Press|date=February 12, 2017|url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/twincities/name/louis-errede-obituary?id=15900395}}</ref>
